children: Kenya has registered a sharp contraction in its elite financial circles, with a massive 300 high-networth individuals dropping off the radar in just 12 months, highlighting the intense macroeconomic pressures facing the East Africa’s largest economy.

The newly released Africa Wealth Report (2026) shows that the country’s population of dollar millionaires holding over $1 million in assets fell 4.41 percent to 6,500 in the 12 months to June 2026 from 6,800 in 2025, while the number of high-net-worth individuals holding more than $100 million in assets declined to 15 from 16 in the same period.

The bulk of the dollar millionaires who dropped off the elite list occurred in Nairobi, where 200 high-net-worth individuals lost their ‘Dollar Millionaire’ tag according to the report by the New World Wealth (NWW), an independent global wealth intelligence and market research form tracking the distribution, movement and spending habits of the world’s wealthiest people.

The total number of wealthy people holding over $1 million worth of assets in Nairobi declined by 5 percent to 4,000 from 4,200, while those commanding over $100 million remained unchanged at 10 during the period under review.

This silent migration of wealth underscores the intense macroeconomic headwinds facing Nairobi where aggressive currency fluctuations, heavy tax burdens, and a shifting investment climate have driven a calculated retreat of local capital.

Despite a tough past two decades, Johannesburg is still the wealthiest city in Africa. The “City of Gold” is the base city for the bulk of the companies listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) Top 40. Much of its wealth is located in the Sandton area, which is widely seen as the “richest square mile in Africa”Kenya’s loss of 300 millionaires is not just a blow to status but also signals less local venture capital investments, fewer high-end property acquisitions, and reduced tax revenues for the country.
It is feared that the rising cost of living, high interest rates, and recent periods of political and social unrest have damaged investor predictability in the country.

Escalating fiscal policies and aggressive tax enforcement over the past year have severely squeezed net corporate margins, and for business owners accustomed to reinvesting pure profit, higher corporate and statutory burdens have constrained local asset growth and suppressed company valuations.

To shield their fortunes from local macroeconomic headwinds, a significant chunk of the country’s elite is, quietly shifting their holdings into safer offshore tax havens, foreign real estate, and hard-currency bonds.

For instance, Kenyan pension funds are moving more retirement savings into global markets, with offshore holdings rising 25 percent in the year to June 2026 to hit Ksh104.99 billion ($810 million) as managers seek protection from domestic risks.
The Retirement Benefits Authority (RBA) shows that offshore investments increased from about Ksh84 billion in June 2025, with global equity trackers attracting new capital.
Kenya retained position five on the list of Africa’s top five wealthiest nations, after South Africa, Egypt, Morocco and Nigeria.

South Africa leads the pack with 48,200 high-net-worth individuals controlling over $1 million worth of assets, 131 individuals with over $100 million in assets and 10 billionaires commanding over $1 billion in assets.

Nigeria has 8,100 millionaires with over $1 million in assets, 22 people with over $100 million in assets and three individuals controlling over $1 billion in assets. Kenya doesn’t have any single dollar billionaire.“Going forward, Africa’s wealth is projected to rise sharply, with millionaire numbers on the continent forecast to more than double by 2040,” the report says“In particular, we expect strong millionaire growth in “lifestyle destinations” such as Cape Town, Marrakech, the Whale Coast, the Garden Route, Tangier, the Cape Winelands, Nairobi, Windhoek and Swakopmund.”“Our projections for Namibia are especially bullish, mainly due to its tax benefits. Notably, Namibia does not tax foreign income and imposes no capital gains tax or estate duty. The capital gains exemption places it in an exclusive group alongside the UAE (United Arab Emirates), the Cayman Islands, Monaco and Singapore.”
